Descriptive source: "បទដ្ឋានអនុវត្តបច្ចេកវិទា ប្រព័ន្ធអន្ទាក់គ្រប់គ្រងសត្វកណ្តុរនៅស្រែ" (Technology Practice Standard: Trap-Barrier System for Rat Management in Rice Fields), Department of Agricultural Extension, MAFF, with CARDI, February 2006.
text:
Building and setting up a Trap-Barrier System (TBS, ធី-ប៊ី-អេស) trap-crop plot for rat management involves three main components: the trap-crop planting, the cage traps, and the plastic barrier.

Trap-crop variety and timing: use a short-duration variety (under about 120 days), non-photoperiod-sensitive, and aromatic - the smell is thought to help attract rats - such as IR66 or Sen Pidor. Nursery seedlings for the trap crop should be raised about 20-25 days before transplanting, started roughly 2-3 weeks earlier than the nursery for the surrounding main crop, so the trap plot heads and ripens ahead of the rest of the field. In the rainy season this timing depends on rainfall; in the dry season it depends on water availability, so farmers may need to raise several small staggered nursery batches (roughly every 10 days) to have suitable seedlings ready whenever conditions allow transplanting.

Cage traps (អងគប់): each cage is built mainly from wire mesh (a coarser mesh for the main body and a finer mesh, illustratively around 4-5mm openings, for the funnel-shaped entrances), plus wire rod for the frame, thin wire for lashings, and bamboo/wood poles for support. A typical cage design uses several funnel-shaped one-way entrances (multiple rats can be caught before the cage needs emptying) and a rear door for removing catches. As an illustrative bill of materials for one cage, this source lists items such as wire mesh (~1.2m for the body plus smaller pieces for entrance funnels), rigid wire rod (~0.5kg) for the frame, thin wire (~0.12kg) for the entrance lashings, string/wire ties, and about 3m of bamboo or reed poles - treat these as approximate quantities to plan around, not exact purchase specifications. A TBS unit typically uses 5-8 cages, placed at intervals around the barrier, with more cages placed at corners or sections where rats are seen concentrating.

Plastic barrier (របាំងផ្លាស្ទិច): the barrier sheet should be a heavy-duty plastic capable of withstanding weather and repeated rat contact - illustratively around 12kg of material can cover roughly 100m of barrier length by this source's estimate, and total barrier length for one 25m x 25m TBS plot is roughly 110m (i.e., the perimeter plus some allowance). Barrier height is roughly 0.7-0.8m. The barrier is reinforced along its top and middle with a rope or cord sewn/threaded through, and supported upright with bamboo poles spaced roughly every 1-1.5m, with the base of the plastic sheet buried a little in the mud so rats cannot burrow underneath. A drainage channel roughly 0.5m wide and somewhat deeper than the surrounding field is dug alongside the barrier, both to help manage water level inside the trap plot and to make it harder for rats to approach the barrier at ground level.

Assembly sequence: dig the drainage channel and set the support poles first, then attach and tension the plastic barrier to the poles (best done by two people - one holding the sheet taut, one securing it - so the barrier lies flat, which reduces gaps rats can exploit), bury the base of the sheet in mud, then position the cages around the perimeter with their entrances facing the barrier at the waterline, baited implicitly by the trap crop's smell, and cover the cages lightly with leaves/vegetation to make the entrance look more natural to approaching rats. Cage installation should be finished by about 10 days after the trap-crop nursery is transplanted into the plot, and in any case before rats begin actively feeding on the ripening trap crop.

Numeric precision caveat: all dimensions, weights, and material quantities above are illustrative planning figures from this source; treat them as a starting point and adjust to local material availability and field conditions rather than exact specifications.
